hypotheses.statement: Being faced with constraints (no choice) strengthens the lay belief in negotiating with fate, relative to choice and neutral conditions, while leaving personal-control and fatalism beliefs unchanged.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: However, the belief in negotiating with fate was stronger in the no-choice condition than in either the neutral [B = -0.24, SE = 0.11, t(194) = 2.18, p = 0.03, d = 0.29] or choice [B = -0.20, SE = 0.09, t(194) = 2.02, p = 0.04, d = 0.29) conditions (see Figure 2). This result replicates the finding from Experiment 1.

hypotheses.statement: Activating the belief in negotiating with fate promotes more adaptive responses to an uncontrollable negative event (less rumination, greater identification of one's own contributing behavior, greater positive reappraisal and acceptance, greater derived meaning) than activating fatalism or personal control.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: With regards to adaptive coping, participants reported significantly greater positive reappraisal of the event after negotiating with fate was activated compared to activating fatalism [B = -0.31, SE = 0.14, t(190) = 2.26, p = 0.03, d = 0.39]

findings.notes: For a one-way ANOVA on three groups, df1 + df2 + 1 = N. F(2,136) therefore implies N = 139, not the 138 given by Study 4's gender and religion blocks. The same batch confirms the df-implied N of 139 matches the education column total of 139 exactly. So two independent routes (the reported degrees of freedom, and the education column) say 139, while two others (gender, religion) say 138. This is a genuine internal ambiguity about Study 4's analytic sample, not a rounding artifact. Innocent explanations exist -- listwise deletion of one participant, or a participant counted in demographics but excluded from the manipulation-check ANOVA -- but none is stated. Note that Experiments 3, 5 and 6 all reconcile exactly (217, 194, 158), so this is not the authors' general convention.

consequence.explanation: Study 4's reported N cannot be pinned to a single value; the manipulation-check F is reported on 139 participants while the table describes 138.

findings.notes: Setting the sign convention aside (see regression_sign_convention), the reported |t| = 2.02 falls just outside the achievable magnitude interval [2.053, 2.412] implied by B = -0.20 and SE = 0.09 at the precision printed. The gap is small (0.033) but the interval already accounts for the full rounding range of both inputs. Notably this is one of the two values the corrigendum specifically revised -- it changed this contrast's p from 0.03 to 0.04 -- so the revised triple still does not fully reconcile. The reported p = 0.04 IS inside its achievable interval, so the discrepancy is confined to the t statistic.

findings.location: Corrigendum, Experiment 5 corrected Results para 3, acceptance negotiating-with-fate vs fatalism contrast
findings.quote: For acceptance, participants reported marginally greater acceptance of the event after negotiating with fate was activated compared to activating fatalism [B = -0.22, SE = 0.11, t(190) = -1.81, p = 0.07, d = 0.10].
findings.reproduction: metascience regression-batch --rows '[{"label":"Exp5 Acceptance NWF vs fatalism","b":-0.22,"se":0.11,"reported_t":-1.81,"reported_p":0.07,"df":190,"decimals_b":2,"decimals_se":2,"decimals_t":2,"decimals_p":2}]'
findings.notes: Unlike the sign-convention rows, this one has matching signs and still fails: t = B/SE = -0.22/0.11 = exactly -2.00, and the achievable interval given the printed precision is [-2.143, -1.870]. The reported -1.81 lies outside it. The recomputed p is 0.047 and the reported p of 0.07 lies outside its achievable interval [0.0334, 0.0631] as well. Both discrepancies point the same way and are larger than rounding permits.

consequence.explanation: B/SE implies p = 0.047, which is significant at alpha = 0.05, whereas the paper reports p = 0.07 and describes the effect as only 'marginally greater'. The reported version is the more conservative one, so this does not inflate the paper's claim -- but the acceptance result's status changes depending on which of the paper's own numbers is trusted.

inputs.family_label: Experiment 2: six regression contrasts (3 lay beliefs x 2 condition comparisons vs no-choice reference) on the same 200 participants

findings.reproduction: metascience multiplicity --family-label 'Experiment 2: six regression contrasts (3 lay beliefs x 2 condition comparisons vs no-choice reference) on the same 200 participants' --tests '[{"id":"e2_fat_neutral","p_value":0.29,"correction_applied":"none"},{"id":"e2_fat_choice","p_value":0.77,"correction_applied":"none"},{"id":"e2_pc_neutral","p_value":0.10,"correction_applied":"none"},{"id":"e2_pc_choice","p_value":0.11,"correction_applied":"none"},{"id":"e2_nwf_neutral","p_value":0.03,"correction_applied":"none"},{"id":"e2_nwf_choice","p_value":0.04,"correction_applied":"none"}]'
findings.notes: These six contrasts are one family on any reasonable reading: three lay beliefs measured on the same 200 participants, each compared against the same no-choice reference group, all bearing on the single hypothesis that constraint shifts fate beliefs. No correction is applied or mentioned. Both significant results (p = 0.03 and p = 0.04) fail every one of the four corrections -- the surviving interval is 0 to 0, identical under Bonferroni, Holm, Benjamini-Hochberg and Benjamini-Yekutieli, so the conclusion does not depend on which method one prefers. Benjamini-Yekutieli is the appropriate reference here because the three belief scales are measured on the same subjects and are certainly correlated. Uncorrected testing is ordinary practice in this literature and this is deterministic arithmetic, not an allegation; but the paper's stated replication claim for Hypothesis 1 rests entirely on these two contrasts.

consequence.explanation: The sentence 'the belief in negotiating with fate was stronger in the no-choice condition than in either the neutral or choice conditions ... This result replicates the finding from Experiment 1' rests on the only two significant p-values in the family, and neither survives correction for the six tests reported alongside them. Computed from 2 result(s) significant uncorrected do not survive correction (a correction the paper did not apply, over a family we chose).

findings.notes: Recorded as an observation about printed literals only. Three patterns in the reported effect sizes invite clarification without any arithmetic being needed to see them. (1) Experiment 2's two contrasts are both given d = 0.29 although their t statistics differ (2.18 and 2.02) at identical df. (2) Within Experiment 5, at identical df = 190, the contrast with the SMALLER |t| of 1.64 carries the LARGER d of 0.28, while |t| = 1.81 carries d = 0.10. unchecked.reason: Deliberately not run. Every mean in these tables is an average of 8, 10 or more Likert items (alpha values are given for 8-, 8- and 10-item scales), so the granularity of a group mean is 1/(k*n) rather than 1/n and the tests have no power; the response-scale bounds are never stated in the corrigendum, so any range would have been invented, which rulebook rule 4 forbids. No power calculation, target effect size or sample-size justification appears anywhere in this corrigendum, so verify_power_analysis had no inputs. Whether the original article states one could not be determined from this document.
